title: Lester's treatment at Fort McClellan: the photo of his white wife
summary: He says Lester was punished after a footlocker search found his wife was white, and Jones was made his guard; Ken Bluett is identified.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Of course not. Three people are alive that will tell you the way they treated Lester Young was horrible. The thing that happened with Lester -
What was the thing, Jo, that happened with Lester?

Oh, the guys pulled up his foot locker and found out his wife was white and they put the 96th Article of War on Lester. The 96th Article covers everything. You have been a soldier, you have been in town, you created a riot, you've stolen, you've killed, you've did everything. That's the biggest thing you can get in the Army. That covers everything and you ain't did nothing, you ain't had a drink yet. Lester hadn't been in town, you see. So the Sergeant said, "You can't do that to this man!" And would you believe that they made me a guard over Lester Young in Fort MacClellan, Alabama. I said, "What do I do now?" He said, "Well, go get my horn." They had him in the prisoner of war thing.
That's right. Major [illegible], that never got a chance to see his wife - he did that. The Captain of the

Company said, "I can't do nothing with this man," 'cause he was a frustrated little young drummer had been in the Army since he was 16 and he was about 25. He says, "What can I do?" and I says, "Nothing you can do." He said, "That man is crazy." He's got 2500 people in there and he's a commissioned officer out of Louisiana. But he got mad at Lester Young because he was married to a white woman. He said, "Who is that?" "That's my wife's picture." "She's a white woman." "Well, that's my wife." And Ken Bluett I had to get in touch with because my Sergeant -
We must identify Ken Bluett. He was the manager of the Regal Theatre in Chicago, which was a black theatre on the south side of 47th and South Parkway.

Mr. Ken Bluett. Everybody that came there, they came from Mr. Ken Bluett. The boy that was the usher was my Sergeant who was scared to tell me to get up in the morning... He was a little young boy that used to run errands and he says, "How can I tell you? You're Count Basie's drummer." I said, "I'm a soldier in the Army." What they did with Lester Young was a horrible thing. Then your life in the U.S. Army
... was not a very thrilling or happy one.
